name: Orkney
title: Orkney Ship Thickness Measurement | Scapa Flow and Kirkwall
description: UTM in Orkney for tankers at Flotta and in Scapa Flow, ferries, cruise ships and accommodation units: deck, tank and piping thickness gauging at anchor.
h1: Ship Gauging in Orkney: Scapa Flow Anchorages, Flotta and Kirkwall
intro: Orkney's waters offer something rare in northern Europe: the huge sheltered anchorage of Scapa Flow, used by tankers loading at the Flotta terminal, by ships transferring cargo from one hull to another, and by accommodation units in for maintenance. Around it, Kirkwall and Stromness serve ferries, cruise ships and the islands' working fleet. A ship lying quietly at anchor in the Flow is a good platform for thickness measurement, and our technicians fly in from India to board her by launch.
keywords: ship to ship transfer tanker inspection
hull gauging at anchor scapa flow

highlights.p: The Flow is enclosed by islands and largely free of swell and tidal stream, so a ship at anchor here is steadier than in most open roadsteads. That makes launch boarding and on-deck gauging practical on days when exposed anchorages elsewhere would be closed to boat work.

Tankers loading at Flotta or arriving for ship-to-ship transfer often anchor for days before their lay-can window or between operations. Time at anchor with cargo or ballast in a known state suits planned deck, piping and ballast tank gauging agreed with the operator.

The ro-pax ferries to Aberdeen and Scrabster, the inter-island ferry fleet and the harbour's tugs and pilot boats all spend predictable time alongside. Their maintenance and lay-over periods are good windows for deck, void-space and sea-water piping work without disrupting timetables.

port.h: Orkney's harbours: Scapa Flow, Kirkwall and Stromness
p: Scapa Flow lies at the heart of the Orkney archipelago, enclosed by Mainland to the north, Hoy to the west and the islands of Flotta, South Ronaldsay and Burray to the south and east. It is one of the largest natural harbours in the world, with deep, sheltered water that served as a fleet anchorage in both world wars. Ships enter through Hoxa Sound in the south, past Flotta, while the Churchill Barriers built during the Second World War close the eastern channels to shipping. Orkney Islands Council is the harbour authority across the islands, providing pilotage, towage, vessel traffic services and counter-pollution cover, and the Flow is the centre of its oil and gas operations. For a visiting ship the result is a large, quiet roadstead with a harbour authority used to tankers.

Oil has shaped the Flow since the Flotta terminal began receiving crude in 1977. Crude oil and LPG arrive through a pipeline of around 210 kilometres from North Sea fields at the terminal on the island of Flotta, where tankers load for export, and field owners have agreed to keep sending production there into the 2030s. Ship-to-ship transfers of crude have taken place in Scapa Flow since 1980 under a council licence, and the Flow handled the world's first LNG ship-to-ship transfer in 2007 and its first LPG transfer in 2016. Since 2015, semi-submersible accommodation units with dynamic positioning have used the Flow for maintenance and crew changes between offshore contracts, holding position or mooring in the sheltered water while work goes on aboard.

Kirkwall is Orkney's capital and its main commercial harbour. The deep-water pier at Hatston, just north of the town, handles the NorthLink ferry on its route between Aberdeen and Lerwick and berths many of the cruise ships that make Orkney a busy cruise destination, while other cruise ships anchor off and tender passengers ashore. Stromness, on the west side of Mainland, takes the ferry from Scrabster across the Pentland Firth and supports marine renewable energy projects testing devices at Orkney's tidal and wave sites. Inter-island ferries link the north and south isles from Kirkwall, Stromness and Houton, and fish farming supports a fleet of workboats. Weather, not ice, is the seasonal limit, with winter gales and short days. Summer brings the busiest cruise programme and the best conditions for boat work.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged in Orkney
p: Orkney has no drydock for seagoing ships, so almost all thickness measurement here happens afloat. In Scapa Flow that means anchorage work: the agent arranges a launch through the harbour authority's marine services, the team boards by pilot or accommodation ladder, and the steadiness of the Flow allows longer working days on board than an open anchorage would. Tankers waiting on lay-can dates, ships between STS operations and accommodation units in for maintenance are the main candidates. Tank entry depends on the ship's own gas-freeing and permits, so the cargo and ballast plan is discussed with the master before the team mobilises.

Alongside work is concentrated at Hatston and Kirkwall piers and at Stromness, where ferries, cruise ships during their calls, and the islands' tugs, pilot boats and workboats lie at predictable times. Ferries and harbour craft that need docking go to yards on the Scottish mainland or further afield, and a gauging visit in Orkney a few weeks before is the practical way to give the yard a measured steel estimate. Accommodation units and project vessels that moor in the Flow rather than on a quay are reached by launch in the same way as the tankers.
list: Scapa Flow anchorages — deck, piping and ballast tank gauging by launch on tankers waiting on lay-can dates or between STS operations.
Flotta terminal — external deck and piping UT on loading tankers, within the terminal's permit and hazardous-area rules.
Accommodation unit moorings in the Flow — pontoon, column and deck gauging on semi-submersibles during maintenance between contracts.
Hatston Pier, Kirkwall — car-deck, void-space and sea-water piping work on ferries and cruise ships during their calls.
Stromness harbour — hull and deck checks on ferries, renewable-energy support vessels and workboats alongside.
Kirkwall harbour — gauging on inter-island ferries, tugs, pilot boats and fish-farm workboats between duties.

context.h: Ship-to-ship transfers, port state control and island regulation
p: Foreign-flagged ships in Orkney waters are subject to port state control by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which continues to apply the Paris MoU under UK legislation. STS operations bring a second layer: in UK territorial waters, cargo transfers between ships are confined to harbour areas holding an approved transfer licence, and Orkney Islands Council's licence for Scapa Flow sets the procedures, weather limits and pollution-response arrangements both ships must follow. Charterers and the oil majors who vet the tankers involved look closely at hull and deck condition, and an STS operation is not the time to discover a leaking deck line.

The islands' own fleets sit under different rules. UK-flagged passenger ferries are surveyed by the MCA for their passenger certificates, fish-farm workboats fall under UK small-vessel codes, and the accommodation units in the Flow are mobile offshore units with their own class and flag requirements. Ballast water is also managed locally: Orkney Islands Council adopted a ballast water management policy for the Flow, reflecting concern about invasive species in waters with important fisheries and fish farms. For an owner, the practical consequence is that the reason for gauging, and the report format needed, can differ from one vessel to the next within a single harbour.

jobs.h: Inspection jobs we see in Orkney
jobs.p: Orkney work is shaped by the Flow. Tankers with time at anchor between operations, accommodation units in for maintenance, and ferries working fixed timetables each offer a different kind of window, and the scope has to suit it. We agree with the superintendent which spaces the crew will prepare, how the team will reach the ship, and what to do if weather or the cargo programme changes the plan. Readings are referenced to frames and strakes as we go, so that a later docking, a vetting inspection or a charter negotiation can rely on them. Where a ship is likely to call again, we suggest how the remaining scope can be completed then.
list: Ballast tank and deck piping gauging on a crude tanker anchored in Scapa Flow ahead of loading at Flotta.
Deck line and manifold area UT on a tanker between ship-to-ship transfers, requested by the charterer's vetting team.
Pontoon, column and bracing inspection with UT and MPI on a semi-submersible accommodation unit during a maintenance period in the Flow.
Car-deck, sea-water piping and void-space gauging on a ro-pax ferry before her winter docking on the mainland.
Hull and deck gauging on an inter-island ferry or fish-farm workboat ahead of a sale or a change of service.

logistics: Kirkwall Airport has Loganair flights from Aberdeen, Edinburgh, Glasgow and Inverness, and the team usually reaches Orkney that way after an international arrival in Scotland. NorthLink ferries from Aberdeen to Kirkwall and from Scrabster to Stromness are useful when equipment travels by road or when flights are weather-bound. The technicians travel from India on UK visas, so early notice of the ship's expected time in the Flow matters. Launches, pier access and any terminal passes are arranged through the ship's agent and the harbour authority.
vessels: Ship-to-ship transfer tankers and gas carriers

faqs.q: Can a tanker be gauged at anchor in Scapa Flow?
faqs.a: Yes. The Flow's shelter makes launch transfers and work on deck practical on more days than an exposed anchorage would allow. Deck plating, deck piping and air pipes can be gauged with the ship in any loading condition, while ballast or cargo tank entry needs the spaces gas-free and certified, which the master arranges. We plan the order of work with the superintendent so the priority readings come first.

faqs.q: Do you inspect tankers involved in ship-to-ship transfers?
faqs.a: Yes, before or between transfers rather than during them. During an STS operation the deck and manifold areas are governed by the transfer's own procedures and the crews are fully occupied. Readings taken while a ship waits in the Flow, on deck lines, manifolds, shell plating where fenders bear and ballast tanks, give the owner evidence for vetting inspectors and charterers who look closely at tankers in STS trades.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Orkney?
faqs.a: Not for seagoing ships. Ferries, tankers and larger workboats dock on the Scottish mainland or at yards abroad. What Orkney offers is sheltered time at anchor or alongside, and readings taken in the Flow or at a pier can be sent to the yard as a pre-docking steel estimate, so renewal is agreed with the class surveyor from measurements rather than assumptions.

faqs.q: Can you inspect semi-submersible accommodation units in Scapa Flow?
faqs.a: Yes, during their maintenance and crew-change periods. Pontoon and column ballast tanks, bracings and deck structure on a semi-submersible see fatigue as well as corrosion, so we combine thickness gauging with magnetic particle testing at welded nodes. The unit's owner arranges tank preparation and access, and we report against the unit's own drawings so findings can be taken into its maintenance records.

faqs.q: How do the islands' weather and daylight affect planning?
faqs.a: Orkney has no sea ice to contend with, but winter gales can stop launch transfers and delay flights, and midwinter daylight is short. We plan a spare day, keep in touch with the agent about the ship's position in the Flow, and schedule outdoor deck work for daylight while tank interiors under lighting fill the dark hours.
